titulo: Who am I: Sein: to be

aula.objetivo: Introduce yourself, ask for someone's name and origin, and use «sein» in the present tense with «du», «ihr» and «Sie».

blocos.contexto: At a language school in Berlin, the teacher welcomes a new student. She addresses him with «Sie». Later he talks to a classmate, using «du».

linhas.ru: — Guten Morgen! Sind Sie Herr Silva?
linhas.pt: — Good morning! Are you Mr. Silva?
linhas.audio: Guten Morgen! Sind Sie Herr Silva?

linhas.ru: — Ja, ich bin Paul Silva. Ich bin aus Brasilien.
linhas.pt: — Yes, I am Paul Silva. I am from Brazil.
linhas.audio: Ja, ich bin Paul Silva. Ich bin aus Brasilien.

linhas.ru: — Freut mich, Herr Silva! Ich bin Frau Becker.
linhas.pt: — Nice to meet you, Mr. Silva! I am Mrs. Becker.
linhas.audio: Freut mich, Herr Silva! Ich bin Frau Becker.

linhas.pt: — Nice to meet you too, Mrs. Becker!

linhas.ru: — Hallo! Ich bin Lea. Bist du auch hier?
linhas.pt: — Hi! I'm Lea. Are you here too?
linhas.audio: Hallo! Ich bin Lea. Bist du auch hier?

linhas.ru: — Ja, ich bin hier. Ich bin ein bisschen müde.
linhas.pt: — Yes, I am here. I am a little tired.
linhas.audio: Ja, ich bin hier. Ich bin ein bisschen müde.

linhas.ru: — Wir sind hier. Wir sind glücklich!
linhas.pt: — We are here. We are happy!
linhas.audio: Wir sind hier. Wir sind glücklich!

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: English uses one verb, «to be», for who you are and how you are. German does the same with «sein», pronounced «zine» (German «s» before a vowel sounds like English «z»). STEP 2: «sein» is irregular, just like English «am / are / is», and it changes a lot. Listen to the forms: «ich bin», «du bist», «er, sie, es ist», «wir sind», «ihr seid», «sie sind». Careful: «sind» sounds like «zint» and «seid» sounds like «zite». STEP 3: use «sein» to say who you are: «Ich bin Brasilianer» or «Das ist Lea». STEP 4: also use it to say how you are or where you are: «Ich bin müde» and «Wir sind hier». Just like English «I am tired» and «We are here». STEP 5: to make a sentence negative, put «nicht» after the verb: «Ich bin nicht müde». STEP 6: in a yes/no question, the verb moves to the front: «Bist du müde?». Answer: «Ja, ich bin müde.» or «Nein, ich bin nicht müde.»
blocos.comparacao: English also has just one verb, «to be», with irregular forms (am, are, is), and German works the same way. The difference is that German has more forms (bin, bist, ist, sind, seid), including separate ones for «du» and «ihr», which English both covers with «you». The forms differ a lot from each other, so you need to memorize them. Questions work just as in English «Are you tired?»: the verb and the pronoun swap places, with no «do»: «Bist du müde?».

erros.motivo: Each person has its own form, just as in English you say «I am», never «I are». With «ich», the form is always «bin».
With «wir», the form is «sind». The form «ist» belongs to «er», «sie» and «es».
The verb stays in second position, and «nicht» comes after it.

blocos.titulo: You, you all, formal you: du, ihr and Sie
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: to talk to ONE person you are close to, such as a friend, a family member, a child or a young colleague, use «du». STEP 2: to talk to SEVERAL people you are close to, use «ihr». STEP 3: to talk to someone you don't know well, or to show respect, use «Sie», pronounced «zee». It works for one or several people. In writing, formal «Sie» always starts with a capital S. STEP 4: with «Sie» the verb has the same form as for «they»: «Sie sind» and «Wie heißen Sie?». STEP 5: when in doubt, use «Sie». The other person will offer you the «du» when they want to.
blocos.comparacao: English has only one «you» for everyone, whether you talk to your best friend, your boss or a whole group. German makes you choose between «du», «ihr» and «Sie», and the choice changes the verb in the whole sentence.

tabela.significado: one person you are close to
several people you are close to

erros.motivo: With «Sie» the verb is plural, even for one person.
With «du», the form of «sein» is «bist». «Sind» belongs to «wir» and «sie».

itens.explicacao: You hear «du bist»: the form «bist» goes with «du». «Ich bin» and «wir sind» sound different.
The beginning is «veer zint»: with «wir», the form is «sind». In «Ihr seid» you would hear «zite».
Write «bin» with «i» and «müde» with «ü». The «ü» is «ee» said with rounded lips, as if you were about to say «oo». You practiced it in lesson 1.
With «ich», the form of «sein» is «bin». The form «bist» belongs to «du» and «ist» to «er».
With «du», the form of «sein» is «bist». The form «bin» belongs to «ich» only.
With «wir», the form is «sind». The form «seid» belongs to «ihr».
With «ihr», you all, the form is «seid». It is the only form that ends in «d» besides «sind».

itens.explicacao: The informal address, for one person you are close to, is «du». «Sie» is formal, and «er» means he, so it is not a direct form of address.

blocos.enunciado: Say out loud: «Ich bin müde. Du bist hier. Wir sind glücklich.». Then ask two yes/no questions with «sein»: one to a friend, «Bist du müde?», and one to a stranger, «Sind Sie müde?».

Look at the tables for the verbs «heißen» and «kommen» from the previous session and say the personal pronouns out loud with their meaning: «ich» (I), «du» (you), «er» (he), «sie» (she), «es» (it), «wir» (we), «ihr» (you all), «sie» (they) and «Sie» (formal you).
